note: Curated starter chunk library. Every entry must be a REUSABLE, generative pattern — never a single fixed sentence. The 10 ids that also exist in curriculum/phrasePatterns.json are kept identical so migrated LanguageGaps merge onto the same chunk.

chunks.meaning: Say which task currently has your attention.
chunks.usage: The default answer when someone asks what you're doing right now.
examples: I'm working on the payment flow.
I'm working on the API cleanup this week.
I'm working on a fix for that crash.

chunks.meaning: It isn't finished yet and you're actively on it.
chunks.usage: Use it when someone expected it to be done — it signals progress without promising completion.
examples: I'm still working on the animation.
I'm still working on it — a couple of edge cases left.
I'm still working on the migration script.

chunks.meaning: Nearly finished, only small things left.
chunks.usage: Softer and more natural than saying a percentage.
examples: I'm almost done with the report.
I'm almost done with it — just cleaning up the tests.
I'm almost done with the first version.

chunks.meaning: Progress matches the plan; the deadline still looks safe.
chunks.usage: Reassures a PM or manager without over-promising.
examples: I'm on track to finish by Thursday.
We're on track to ship this sprint.
I'm on track to have it ready for review tomorrow.

chunks.phrase: I haven't had much time to...
chunks.pattern: I haven't had much time to + VERB
chunks.meaning: You haven't been able to get to it yet, without sounding like an excuse.
chunks.usage: The natural workplace alternative to "I don't have enough time to...".
examples: I haven't had much time to look into it.
I haven't had much time to review the PR yet.
I haven't had much time to dig into the logs.

chunks.pattern: I'm not sure how to + VERB
chunks.meaning: You don't know the best way to do something.
chunks.usage: Admits uncertainty about method without sounding incapable.
examples: I'm not sure how to explain it clearly.
I'm not sure how to reproduce the bug.
I'm not sure how to bring it up with the client.

chunks.meaning: You don't know whether something is true or will happen.
chunks.usage: Use it to flag doubt before committing to an answer.
examples: I'm not sure if that's the root cause.
I'm not sure if we can make it by Friday.
I'm not sure if she's already seen the message.

chunks.meaning: You don't know which thing / which action applies.
chunks.usage: The natural fix for "I don't know what should I do."
examples: I'm not sure what we should do next.
I'm not sure what's causing it.
I'm not sure what he meant by that.

chunks.meaning: A softer, slightly more hedged version of "I'm not sure".
chunks.usage: Good when you want to sound thoughtful rather than blank.
examples: I'm not quite sure yet — let me check.
I'm not quite sure that's the whole picture.
I'm not quite sure how long it'll take.

chunks.meaning: You're confirming your understanding before moving on.
chunks.usage: Prevents misunderstandings without implying the other person was unclear.
examples: Just to make sure I understand, you want the old flow removed?
Just to make sure we're aligned — this ships next week?
Just to make sure, should I include the mobile version too?

chunks.pattern: I want to make sure + CLAUSE
chunks.meaning: You're signalling that getting this right matters to you.
chunks.usage: Slightly more deliberate than "Just to make sure...".
examples: I want to make sure I understand the requirement.
I want to make sure we're not duplicating work.
I want to make sure this is what you had in mind.

chunks.meaning: Check a specific interpretation of what was just said.
chunks.usage: More natural than "What is your meaning?".
examples: Do you mean the whole page, or just the header?
Do you mean we should postpone the release?
Do you mean the staging environment?

chunks.meaning: Politely ask for a vague point to be made specific.
chunks.usage: Works well in meetings and with clients.
examples: Could you clarify what you mean by "soon"?
Could you clarify which part is blocking?
Could you clarify the scope a bit?

chunks.meaning: Ask someone to walk you through something.
chunks.usage: The preposition matters — "explain me this" is a very common mistake.
examples: Could you explain this requirement to me?
Can you explain the flow to the new engineer?
Let me explain the trade-off to the team.

chunks.phrase: We're running into an issue with...
chunks.pattern: running into an issue with + NOUN
chunks.meaning: Report a problem that has come up during the work.
chunks.usage: Neutral framing — states the problem without assigning blame.
examples: We're running into an issue with the payment provider.
I'm running into an issue with the build.
We ran into an issue with the migration last night.

chunks.meaning: Point at the single most important part of a problem.
chunks.usage: Use it to cut through a messy explanation.
examples: The main issue is that the API times out under load.
The main issue is the missing test data.
The main issue is we don't have access yet.

chunks.meaning: Something is giving you difficulty right now.
chunks.usage: Honest and natural — better than "I have a difficulty".
examples: I'm having trouble with the deployment script.
I'm having trouble with the new auth flow.
I'm having trouble with getting it to run locally.

chunks.meaning: Offer a likely explanation without claiming certainty.
chunks.usage: Very common when reporting findings that aren't confirmed yet.
examples: It looks like the issue is in the animation layer.
It looks like the cache isn't being cleared.
It looks like it only happens on mobile.

chunks.meaning: Your progress depends on someone or something else.
chunks.usage: The preposition is required — "waiting the feedback" is a common mistake. "Waiting on" also works.
examples: I'm waiting for the UX feedback.
I'm waiting on Alex to review the PR.
We're waiting for the client to confirm.

chunks.meaning: Float an idea without pushing it.
chunks.usage: Low-pressure way to open a suggestion in a meeting.
examples: Maybe we could split it into two tickets.
Maybe we could ship the basic version first.
Maybe we could ask design for a quick review.

chunks.pattern: One option would be to + VERB
chunks.meaning: Present one possibility among several.
chunks.usage: Signals you've thought about alternatives — good with managers.
examples: One option would be to push the feature to the next release.
One option would be to cache the results.
One option would be to handle it manually for now.

chunks.meaning: Invite the other person to consider an idea with you.
chunks.usage: More collaborative than stating the suggestion flatly.
examples: What if we move the deadline by a week?
What if we only support the top three browsers?
What if we ask the client first?

chunks.phrase: I'm not sure that's the best approach.
chunks.pattern: I'm not sure that's the best + NOUN
chunks.meaning: Disagree without saying "no" or "you're wrong".
chunks.usage: The standard soft disagreement in professional English.
examples: I'm not sure that's the best approach for mobile.
I'm not sure that's the best option right now.
I'm not sure that's the best place to put it.

chunks.pattern: I see your point, but + CLAUSE
chunks.meaning: Acknowledge their view before offering yours.
chunks.usage: Keeps disagreement collaborative rather than confrontational.
examples: I see your point, but that would delay the release.
I see your point, but we'd have to rewrite the parser.
I see your point — I'm just worried about the timeline.

chunks.pattern: I'm a little concerned about + NOUN
chunks.meaning: Raise a worry gently.
chunks.usage: "A little" does the softening — it makes a strong concern sayable.
examples: I'm a little concerned about the performance impact.
I'm a little concerned about the timeline.
I'm a little concerned about how this scales.

chunks.phrase: I should have it done by...
chunks.meaning: Give a completion date with a little room.
chunks.usage: "by Friday" means on or before Friday; "until Friday" is a common mistake here.
examples: I should have it done by Friday.
I can get it to you by the end of the day.
We should have the fix out by tomorrow morning.

chunks.pattern: We should be able to + VERB
chunks.meaning: Likely, but not a hard promise.
chunks.usage: Useful when you're fairly confident but don't want to commit absolutely.
examples: We should be able to finish this sprint.
I should be able to get to it this afternoon.
We should be able to support both formats.

chunks.meaning: State your target date as a goal, not a guarantee.
chunks.usage: Honest framing when the date could still move.
examples: I'm aiming for Friday.
We're aiming for the end of the week.
I'm aiming to have a draft ready tomorrow.

chunks.meaning: Give a rough estimate of time or size.
chunks.usage: Common when the number is approximate.
examples: We're looking at about two weeks.
We're looking at early next month.
We're probably looking at a couple more days.

chunks.phrase: Have you had a chance to...?
chunks.pattern: Have you had a chance to + VERB?
chunks.meaning: Ask whether someone has done something, without pressuring them.
chunks.usage: The polite way to chase something — it builds in the excuse of being busy.
examples: Have you had a chance to look at the PR?
Have you had a chance to review the doc?
Have you had a chance to talk to the client yet?

chunks.phrase: I wanted to follow up on...
chunks.meaning: Reopen something that was discussed before.
chunks.usage: Standard opener for a chasing message or a second conversation.
examples: I wanted to follow up on the design feedback.
Just following up on my message from yesterday.
I'm following up on the access request.

chunks.meaning: Commit to investigating without promising a fix yet.
chunks.usage: "Look into" is much more natural than "investigate" in everyday work talk.
examples: I'll look into it this afternoon.
Let me look into the error logs.
I'll look into why it's failing on mobile.

chunks.phrase: I'll get back to you on that.
chunks.pattern: get back to + PERSON + on + TOPIC
chunks.meaning: You'll answer later once you know more.
chunks.usage: Buys time politely instead of guessing.
examples: I'll get back to you on that by tomorrow.
Let me check and get back to you.
I'll get back to you once I've talked to the team.

chunks.phrase: Could you take a look at...?
chunks.meaning: Ask someone to review or check something.
chunks.usage: Lighter than "review" — easy to say no to, so it feels less demanding.
examples: Could you take a look at this when you get a chance?
Do you mind taking a look at the PR?
Can you take a look at the error I'm getting?
